title: What Medieval Kyiv Looked Like 1,000 Years Ago Before History Forgot It (AI Reconstruction)
fullText: Kiev. The year is 972. On the steppe north of the Black Sea, a Pecheneg chieftain raises a cup of polished gold and drinks to the birth of strong sons. The cup is not metal. It is a human skull — reshaped, lined in gold leaf, given to him by his own men. The dead man inside was Sviatoslav, prince of Kiev. His demise will set in motion a chain of events so violent that within sixteen years, his youngest son will baptize an empire by drowning his own gods. Before that baptism, Kiev was a fortress of wood where a single prince kept eight hundred concubines in three palaces around the city. Before its cathedrals rose above the Dnieper, it was the largest slave market in eastern Europe. Before later centuries claimed its name, Kiev was something stranger. The Viking capital of the Slavic world. A city growing fast enough to overtake Paris and London. I'm Arthur, and what follows belongs to no modern country. It is the story of a Slavic-Viking- Byzantine hybrid that became medieval Europe's largest empire — and in one generation, sowed the seeds of its own collapse. This is Kiev. The city that drowned its own gods. The year is 980. A young warlord rides south through the forests of the Rus toward Kiev, leading an army of Scandinavian mercenaries he spent two winters recruiting. His name is Vladimir. He is the youngest son of the prince who became a cup. And he is not supposed to be here. His mother was a slave in the prince's household. After his father died, Vladimir watched his older brothers turn against each other. One was crushed in retreat under his own men in a fortress moat. The other, Yaropolk, seized Kiev. Vladimir fled across the Baltic, gathered Viking warriors loyal to silver, and came back to claim what no one believed he could take. On his march south, he stopped at Polotsk and offered a marriage alliance to its princess, Rogneda. Her answer was preserved word for word, nearly a thousand years later. I will not unshoe the son of a slave. In the marriage customs of that world, the bride removed her husband's boots on the wedding night as a sign of submission. Rogneda's refusal could only be answered one way. Vladimir stormed Polotsk, claimed her father's life before her very eyes, and took her as his prize. He moved on the same week. At the gates of Kiev, the pattern repeated. Vladimir could not breach the wooden walls, so he bribed Yaropolk's most trusted advisor to lure his brother out under a false offer of peace. When Yaropolk entered Vladimir's tent to negotiate, two Norse mercenaries ended his reign before he could speak. By the end of 980, Vladimir ruled the Rus alone. He kept eight hundred concubines distributed across three palaces. He raised six wooden idols on the highest hill of Kiev. At their center stood Perun, god of thunder, his head plated in silver, his moustache gilded in gold. For later chroniclers, this Vladimir was a kind of dark double. A Slavic Solomon who lived for appetites alone. But violence could not give him what he wanted next. To be treated as an equal by the emperor in Constantinople, he would need something violence could not produce. He would need a god. And the god he chose would not be one of the six he had set on his own hill. In 988, Vladimir made a move no one expected. He attacked the Byzantine Empire — not as a raider, but as a buyer. He marched on Kherson, in Crimea, and held it as ransom. His demand was insolent. He wanted the hand of Anna, sister of the emperors Basil and Constantine. The highest-ranking unmarried woman in the Christian world. No princess of her rank had ever been sent to a foreign court. The emperors said yes anyway. They had a civil war to win, and Vladimir was offering six thousand Viking warriors as part of the deal. Those warriors would become the famous Varangian Guard — the personal bodyguards of the Byzantine emperor for the next four hundred years. So Anna was sent north, the warriors south, and Vladimir was baptized in Kherson. Then he came home to baptize a kingdom. What followed is one of the most cinematic scenes in any medieval chronicle. The same Perun that Vladimir had raised on the hill eight years earlier was now dragged down to the river by Vladimir's own warriors. Twelve men walked alongside the idol with wooden clubs, beating it as it went. Their orders were specific. The idol was not allowed to stop. Anywhere the dragging slowed, the clubs came down. The pagan crowd followed the god to the bank of the Dnieper, weeping and crying, Perun, save us. The river took the idol south, and the crowd ran along the shore as long as they could, until it was gone. The point of the spectacle was theological. Vladimir was not merely destroying foreign gods. He was destroying his own — the centralized pagan religion he himself had designed less than a decade earlier. The man who had drowned Perun was the same man who had crowned him. Then the campaign moved north. In Novgorod, Vladimir sent his uncle Dobrynya and a commander named Putyata with armed men. The temple of Perun was burned to the ground. Hundreds of resisters perished or driven into the forests. A grim proverb circulated through the Rus for generations. Putyata baptized with the sword, and Dobrynya with fire. In the city, the new religion took quickly. In the countryside, it didn't. For centuries afterward, a kind of double faith persisted across the Rus. Peasants kept calling on Perun for thunder and on the earth-mother Mokosh for safe childbirth, just under the names of new saints. Perun became Saint Elijah. Mokosh slipped quietly into the figure of the Virgin. The wound in the spiritual life of the Rus would not close for hundreds of years. The river had carried the old gods south. But on the same river, in the same week, ships were already coming north — bringing the trade that had built Kiev in the first place. And its most valuable cargo was not amber, or fur, or silver. It was people. Walk down from the prince's hill in the year 1000 and the air changes immediately. The Podol is the river-port at the foot of the city. A strip of mud and timber along the Dnieper where the entire wealth of the Rus passes through every spring and autumn. Smoke from birch fires. Fermented honey from beer-halls. Wet fur. And underneath everything, the smell of tar from the longships. This is the Kiev that mattered to the world. Not the cathedrals. The cargo. For nearly two centuries, the route running through it was the most lucrative trade corridor in northern Europe. It started in the Baltic and emerged at the head of the Dnieper, joining the Vikings of Scandinavia to the markets of Constantinople. Two thousand kilometers from end to end. The Greeks called the Norse who walked it the Varangians. The Slavs called the road itself the Way from the Varangians to the Greeks. Stand at the wharf and watch the cargo coming up the river. Pelts of marten and slate. Sacks of wax and honey — the candles and sweetener of medieval Europe. But more than half the trade — close to half the entire fortune of the Rus — moved in chains. Slavic captives, taken in raids on the inland tribes, marched in lines down to the docks to be sold. A geographer of this period describes the scene. An Arab merchant on the wharf, counting one hundred and eighty silver dirhams from his belt- purse. In front of him, chained to a post, a Slavic girl of perhaps sixteen waited to learn whether she would be sent to Constantinople — where she would be worth three times as much — or down the Volga to the markets of Baghdad. The river was death twice over. Below Kiev, the Dnieper passed through seven sets of rapids. Narrow, boulder-strewn channels where every spring the ships had to be unloaded and dragged overland on logs. In a bad year, between twenty and thirty percent of all vessels on the route never made it through. They broke apart in the white water, or were ambushed on the portage trails by Pecheneg raiders who knew exactly where the merchants would have to come ashore. The people they called Varangians were, by this point, mostly not Vikings at all. Burial digs show that by 1010, eight out of every ten warriors in the prince's guard had Slavic mothers or Slavic wives. They wore amber crosses and silver hammers of Thor on the same chain around the neck. Inside a wooden house at the edge of the Podol, you can find the spiritual reality of the city in a single gesture. A weaver kneels at her loom in the early morning. She whispers a prayer to Mokosh, the old goddess of fate, as she begins the first thread. This is the wealth and the silence in which the Rus lived for the next quarter century. Then, in the summer of 1015, the prince who had drowned the old gods died in his own bed. His sons opened his will. And the purge began. Vladimir had at least a dozen sons when he died. Three of them mattered. The oldest claimant was Sviatopolk, a son his father had never trusted. He moved first. Before Vladimir's body was cold, he seized the throne and sent word to his half-brothers that he would honor them as fellow princes — if they came to swear loyalty. The first half-brother was named Boris. He was camped with his small army on the river Alta, returning from a campaign against the steppe. When messengers warned him that assassins were already on the road, his soldiers begged him to march on Kiev and take the throne by force. He refused. He would not draw a sword against his own brother. He sent his army home, kept only a handful of servants, and waited in his tent. That night the assassins came. They cut their way in. Boris was still breathing when they carried his body away, to make sure no one could claim he was alive. His Hungarian servant George threw his body across the prince to shield him, and was killed for a gold necklace he was wearing. The second brother was Gleb. He was sailing down the river toward Kiev, not yet knowing his father was dead, when a message reached him from his sister. Turn back. Boris was already gone. Sviatopolk had sent men for him as well. His boat was overtaken before he could escape. The killers did not do the work themselves. They forced his own cook, a man named Torchin, to draw his blade and strike the prince. Torchin obeyed. The reason these two killings are remembered is not their violence. The age was full of violence. They are remembered because of what Boris and Gleb did not do. Neither lifted a weapon. Neither tried to flee with an army. Both accepted death rather than start a war between brothers. Within a generation, they became the first canonized saints of the Slavic Christian world. Passion-bearers, the church called them. Men who suffered rather than struck back. Two princes who refused to kill became the first martyrs of the faith their father had imposed by drowning. What followed was nearly four years of civil war. Vladimir's surviving son by Rogneda — Yaroslav, prince of Novgorod — gathered a Viking-Slavic army and marched south. The last battle, on the same river Alta where Boris had been killed, lasted from sunrise to dusk. By nightfall Sviatopolk's army was broken. He fled west into Polish territory and was dead within a year. History remembers him by a single name. Sviatopolk the Cursed. Yaroslav inherited a kingdom soaked in the blood of his own family. The first thing he did was write down the law. Until that moment, the central legal institution of Slavic society had been blood vengeance. Yaroslav's code did something almost unimaginable. It replaced the blade with a price. Every act of violence now had a fee paid to the prince, and the prince settled. The grandfather had changed the gods of the Rus. The grandson changed its laws. For almost two decades, Yaroslav fought to hold the borders he had inherited. He pushed Polish armies out of Galicia. He beat back the steppe tribes year after year. And then, a generation after the civil war, the steppe came at him one last time. The Pechenegs had haunted the south for a hundred years. They had killed Yaroslav's grandfather, the one who became a cup. They had raided the slave caravans on the rapids. They had taken silver and salt and lives from every prince of Kiev in living memory. In 1036, while Yaroslav was in Novgorod, they came at the capital itself — betting they could take the city while its ruler was a thousand kilometers away. Yaroslav rode hard for ten days and reached Kiev before the walls fell. He met the Pechenegs on the open ground south of the city. The fighting lasted from dawn until the last hour of light. By evening, the steppe army was broken so completely that the Pechenegs as a political force never recovered. The southern frontier of the Rus, the bleeding wound of a century, was sealed in a single afternoon. The next thing Yaroslav did, he did on purpose. He ordered the foundations of the largest church in the Slavic world to be laid on the exact ground where his army had cut down the Pechenegs the day before. The cathedral was called Saint Sophia, after the great Byzantine church in Constantinople. Its architects, its mosaicists, its mortar — all imported from the south. Inside, beneath the dome, Yaroslav would stand on a floor laid over the unburied bones of the steppe. The gods of the Pechenegs had failed on that ground. Now a Christian dome rose above them. The building was a statement, and everyone who entered understood it. Saint Sophia of Kiev rose with thirteen domes — one for Christ, twelve for the apostles. The walls shimmered with gold mosaic from floor to dome. Above the altar, the figure of the Virgin in prayer was set in tiles of glass and gold so fine that Kievans claimed they could feel her watching them from anywhere on the floor. Around it, Yaroslav rebuilt the city itself. He extended the walls of Kiev nearly tenfold. He pierced the new wall with a single ceremonial entrance — the Golden Gate, modeled openly on the Golden Gate of Constantinople. The envoys who entered Kiev under that arch were meant to remember the arch they had walked through in their own capital. Kiev was no longer asking permission to be considered part of the Christian world. It was reminding the Christian world that it was already inside. And then, in 1051, Yaroslav did something no one in the Slavic east had ever dared. He appointed a priest from Kiev — a Slav, not a Greek — as the new metropolitan of the Rus, by his own authority, without asking the Patriarch of Constantinople for permission first. He simply told the council of bishops to do it, and they did. From that day, the church of Kiev answered to Kiev. But statements in stone and statements in church were not the only statements Yaroslav had made. Eight years earlier, he had tried to give the Slavic state its own teeth. He had sent two hundred ships against Constantinople itself. The year was 1043, and Yaroslav was running out of patience. A trade dispute had soured in the imperial capital. A Rus merchant had been killed in a street fight. The compensation owed under old treaties was refused. Yaroslav decided the moment had come to remind Constantinople of the same lesson his great-grandfather had taught two centuries earlier — that the Vikings of Kiev still knew the road to the Greeks. He sent his son Vladimir down the Dnieper at the head of nearly two hundred ships and thousands of warriors. They reached the Bosphorus in late summer. The Byzantine navy met them with the most feared weapon of the age — Greek fire. A liquid sprayed from the bows of warships that burned on water and could not be put out. The Rus fleet was destroyed. Thousands of the prince's men were lost in the strait. Vladimir himself escaped on a fishing boat. It was the last major war Kiev ever fought with Constantinople. It ended in disaster. But the Byzantines understood the message, even in victory. Three years later, the empire that had just burned a Rus fleet sat down to negotiate. The treaty was sealed by the marriage of one of Yaroslav's younger sons to a Byzantine princess. Yaroslav had lost the battle. He had won the only thing he had ever wanted — recognition. The emperor of Constantinople was now his in-law. The humiliation in the strait had purchased a diplomatic seat the Rus would never have been offered without first proving they could threaten it. Yaroslav had at least three daughters, and he turned them into a foreign policy. The first married the king of Norway. the second married the king of Hungary. The third — Anna Yaroslavna — was sent west. To a kingdom that fifty years earlier no one in Kiev had even cared about. France. In 1051, Anna was crowned queen consort of Henry the First of France at the cathedral of Reims. She was twenty-two. She brought with her a Slavic-Greek Gospel, bound in jeweled covers, on which the kings of France would swear their coronation oaths for the next six hundred years. There is a parchment in the French archives from a few years later. It is a royal grant. At the bottom of the document, in a court where Latin was the language of state and most of the lay nobility relied on clergy to read and write for them, the queen signed her name herself. In Slavic letters, not Latin. Three Cyrillic characters, spelling out the sound of her name and her title. Ana R'ina. Anna, the Queen. A Slavic queen had taken a Latin throne. She signed in the alphabet of her grandfather's gods. Back in Kiev, the man who had sent her west was finishing his work. A German chronicler named Adam of Bremen called Kiev in this period the ornament of Greece — the rival, he said, of the imperial city itself. By the early 1050s, the empire Yaroslav governed stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Roughly one and a half million square kilometers — larger than the Holy Roman Empire of the same year. But Yaroslav was old, and he knew what was coming. On his deathbed in the winter of 1054, he gathered his sons and dictated a will. Kiev to the eldest, Iziaslav. Chernigov to the second, Pereyaslavl to the third. The lesser cities to the younger boys. And when each prince died, the others would move up by seniority. Every brother climbing one rung at a time. The system was called the lestvitsa — the ladder. He believed it would prevent civil wars. It produced them. Less than twenty years after his death, two of his sons were already at war with the third. By the next generation, the Rus had broken into more than a dozen rival principalities. By the next century, an army of horsemen from the eastern steppe would ride into a city no longer capable of defending itself. None of that had happened yet. Yaroslav was laid in a stone sarcophagus beneath the mosaic of the Virgin he had built. A boatman on the Podol, named only in passing in the chronicle, looked up the hill at the funeral and said the prince who united the route was gone. He was right. The route would never be united again. Three generations. Between a grandfather drunk from as a cup on the steppe — and a granddaughter signing her name as Queen of France at a cathedral in Reims. Seventy-four years. Most of what they built is gone. The wooden palaces burned in the fires of later wars. The Golden Gate stands in fragments behind glass. Saint Sophia survives, but stripped, modified, contested. The Viking warriors are silt in a riverbed. The skull cup of Sviatoslav was either lost or destroyed. The Pecheneg tribes who drank from it were shattered into history. But that one parchment is still in France. Ana R'ina. Three Cyrillic letters on a Latin grant. A queen signing in the alphabet of a people whose own great-grandfather had been used as a goblet by a horseman on the steppe, on a French altar fifteen years before the Normans crossed the Channel. The Holy Roman Empire of her year was smaller than her father's territory. Kiev was not on the edge of Europe. Kiev was a capital. And history has been forgetting that ever since. We just saw a princess of Kiev become Queen of France, taking her Slavic letters to the west. But what was happening in the French capital a few centuries later? Paris went through a century of shadows, facing plagues and wild wolves in its streets. Watch the story of Paris to see how a city survives its darkest era. Subscribe to the channel, and let's keep reviving the past. See you on the next journey. Before we finish, I want to take a moment to recognize the people appearing on screen right now. To the members of this channel, thank you so much. Your ongoing support is what motivates me and helps keep this project alive. If you enjoy what we do here and would like to directly support the channel, I invite you to click the join button down below. To our members, and to everyone who is simply watching this video, thank you for your time.
fullTextVi: Kiev. Năm là 972. Trên thảo nguyên phía bắc Biển Đen, một thủ lĩnh người Pecheneg nâng cốc vàng đánh bóng và đồ uống cho sự ra đời của những đứa con trai khỏe mạnh. Chiếc cốc không phải là kim loại. Đó là một hộp sọ người — được định hình lại, dát vàng lá, đưa cho anh ta bởi chính người của mình. Người chết bên trong là Sviatoslav, hoàng tử Kiev. Cái chết của anh ta sẽ mở ra một chuỗi sự kiện bạo lực đến mức bên trong mười sáu tuổi, đứa con trai út của ông sẽ rửa tội cho một đế chế bằng cách nhấn chìm các vị thần của chính mình. Thủ đô Viking của thế giới Slav. Một thành phố phát triển đủ nhanh để vượt qua Paris và London. Tôi là Arthur, và những gì tiếp theo không thuộc về đất nước hiện đại nào cả. Thành phố đã nhấn chìm các vị thần của chính nó. Năm là 980. Một lãnh chúa trẻ cưỡi ngựa về phía nam xuyên qua những khu rừng của Rus tới Kiev, dẫn đầu một đội quân đánh thuê Scandinavia mà ông đã dành hai mùa đông để tuyển mộ. Tên anh ấy là Vladimir. Anh là con trai út của hoàng tử đã trở thành một chiếc cốc. Và anh ấy không được phép ở đây. Mẹ anh là nô lệ trong gia đình hoàng tử. Người còn lại, Yaropolk, chiếm giữ Kiev. Vladimir chạy trốn qua biển Baltic, tập hợp các chiến binh Viking trung thành với bạc và quay trở lại để đòi lại thứ mà không ai tin rằng anh ta có thể lấy được. Trên đường hành quân về phía nam, anh ta dừng lại ở Polotsk và đề nghị kết hôn với công chúa của nó, Rogneda. Câu trả lời của cô được lưu giữ từng chữ, gần một nghìn năm sau. Tôi sẽ không cởi giày cho con trai của một nô lệ. Theo phong tục cưới xin của thế giới đó, cô dâu cởi bốt của chồng đêm tân hôn như một dấu hiệu của sự phục tùng. Sự từ chối của Rogneda chỉ có thể được đáp lại một chiều. Vladimir xông vào Polotsk, cướp đi mạng sống của cha cô ngay trước mắt cô và bắt cô như phần thưởng của mình. Anh ấy chuyển đi trong cùng một tuần. Tại cổng Kiev, mô hình đó lặp lại. Vladimir không chọc thủng được bức tường gỗ nên đã hối lộ cố vấn thân tín nhất của Yaropolk để dụ anh trai mình ra ngoài theo một lời đề nghị hòa bình giả tạo. Khi Yaropolk vào lều của Vladimir để đàm phán, hai lính đánh thuê Bắc Âu đã kết thúc triều đại của ông ta trước anh ấy có thể nói được. Đến cuối năm 980, Vladimir một mình cai trị Rus. Để được hoàng đế ở Constantinople đối xử bình đẳng, anh ta sẽ cần một cái gì đó bạo lực không thể tạo ra. Anh ta sẽ cần một vị thần. Và vị thần anh chọn sẽ không phải là một trong sáu vị thần anh có đặt trên ngọn đồi của riêng mình. Năm 988, Vladimir đã có một động thái không ai ngờ tới. Anh ta muốn có bàn tay của Anna, em gái của hoàng đế Basil và Constantine. Người phụ nữ chưa lập gia đình có địa vị cao nhất trong thế giới Cơ đốc giáo. Chưa có công chúa nào cùng đẳng cấp với cô từng bị đưa tới triều đình nước ngoài. Dù sao thì các hoàng đế cũng nói có. Họ có một cuộc nội chiến để giành chiến thắng và Vladimir đã đưa ra sáu nghìn Viking chiến binh như một phần của thỏa thuận. Những chiến binh đó sẽ trở thành Đội cận vệ Varangian nổi tiếng - vệ sĩ riêng của Hoàng đế Byzantine trong bốn trăm năm tiếp theo. Vì vậy, Anna được gửi về phía bắc, các chiến binh về phía nam, và Vladimir được rửa tội ở Kherson. Sau đó ông trở về nhà để rửa tội cho một vương quốc. Những gì tiếp theo là một trong những cảnh điện ảnh nhất trong bất kỳ biên niên sử thời Trung cổ nào. Perun mà Vladimir đã nuôi trên đồi tám năm trước là giờ đây đã bị chính chiến binh của Vladimir kéo xuống sông. Mười hai người đàn ông đi bên cạnh thần tượng bằng gậy gỗ, đánh nó khi nó đi.
